name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,232

clue.text: Two personal assistants for old man

blocks.note: the usual abbreviation for a personal assistant
'Two' asks for the same abbreviation a second time

explanation.surface: An elderly man is being looked after by a pair of helpers.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests carers for an old man; in fact the two assistants simply sit side by side and spell him.
explanation.definitionFit: Papa is an informal word for father, and 'old man' is slang for one's father.

clue.text: US state harbouring resistance fighter

blocks.note: Maine is a US state
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: A state is sheltering a member of an armed resistance movement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resistance fighter' reads as one phrase, a partisan; the split falls between the two words, with resistance giving R and fighter the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A marine is a soldier serving with a navy, so a fighter.

clue.text: Depart NY in turmoil, splitting hairs

indicators.note: letters in turmoil are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: the eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone leaves New York in a state of agitation, tearing their hair out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Splitting hairs' looks like a continuation of the turmoil, but it is the definition; NY supplies letters, not a city.
explanation.definitionFit: Splitting hairs is fussing over tiny distinctions, which is what pedantry is.

clue.text: Contact attendant at court

blocks.note: the verb for summoning someone over a loudspeaker or beeper
a royal court, not a law court: the boy who waits on a monarch or noble

explanation.surface: Getting in touch with an official who works at a law court.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's court is a law court, but the second definition is a royal court, where a page is a young attendant.
explanation.definitionFit: To page someone is to contact them by call or pager; a page is a boy attendant to a monarch or noble.

clue.text: Policeman, one managing to acquire power

blocks.note: a coper is one who copes, that is, manages
P is the symbol for power

explanation.surface: A police officer, or a manager, gets hold of power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One managing' reads like a manager in charge; it is COPER, someone who copes.
explanation.definitionFit: Copper is informal British slang for a police officer.

clue.text: No crossword setter could be so ignorant

blocks.note: read literally: a setter's whole job is writing hints for solvers, so one without any would have nothing to publish
the plain sense: an everyday word for knowing nothing, built on the very thing setters write

explanation.surface: A jab at a puzzle-maker: nobody who sets crosswords could be that dim.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is cryptic: a setter who was clue-less would have nothing to set. The second half is the straight meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses at once: literally lacking clues, and the informal word for having no idea at all.

clue.text: Is monkey allowed to eat this?

definitions.text: Is monkey allowed to eat this?

blocks.note: 'Is ... allowed' turned into a question becomes CAN
an ape is a monkey in crossword terms

explanation.surface: A zookeeper is asked whether the monkey may have this snack.
explanation.walkthrough: Put as a question, 'Is monkey allowed?' is 'Can ape?', and the whole clue then describes a thing to eat.
explanation.definitionFit: A canape is a small savoury snack, something one eats.

clue.text: A vote, initially on name for space programme

indicators.note: 'initially on' asks for the first letter of on

blocks.note: the article as printed
a poll is a vote
the first letter of on

explanation.surface: A ballot is being held to pick a name for a space mission.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's vote on a name is exactly how the letters build: A, then POLL, then the O that starts on.
explanation.definitionFit: Apollo was the NASA programme that landed astronauts on the Moon.

clue.text: Confirm live data needs correcting

indicators.note: letters that need correcting are in the wrong order and must be rearranged

blocks.note: the eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An instruction to check that live data is correct before using it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a data engineer's to-do item; 'live data' is only the letters for the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To validate something is to confirm that it is correct or sound.

clue.text: Support nobleman when caught

indicators.note: a word caught by the ear is heard

blocks.note: a British lord, such as a duke or earl, is a peer; the sound is kept and respelt

explanation.surface: A lord is propped up after being arrested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' suggests an arrest or a catch at cricket; here it means caught by the ear.
explanation.definitionFit: A pier is a pillar supporting a bridge or arch, so a support.

clue.text: Abandon the Sahara?

blocks.note: the verb, as a soldier leaving his post without permission
the vast dry, sandy expanse across North Africa, a definition by example

explanation.walkthrough: The two senses are pronounced differently: to deSERT is to abandon, and a DESert is a dry region such as the Sahara.
explanation.definitionFit: One word, two stresses: a verb that is a plain synonym for abandon, and a noun for which the Sahara is the textbook example.

clue.text: Ultimate net value to be adjusted

indicators.note: the letters are to be adjusted into a new order

blocks.note: the eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An accountant's final net figure still needs adjusting.
explanation.walkthrough: The accounting surface hides that 'net value' is just the eight letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Ultimate and eventual both mean happening at the end.

clue.text: Quietly recommend expulsion

blocks.note: p (piano) means quietly in music
to urge is to recommend strongly

explanation.surface: Someone discreetly suggests that a member be thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quietly' looks like an adverb for recommend; it is the musical P.
explanation.definitionFit: A purge is the expulsion of unwanted people from a group.

clue.text: What you might have at breakfast time in prison?

definitions.text: What you might have at breakfast time in prison?

blocks.clueFragment: What you might have at breakfast
blocks.note: the surface reading: a bowl of hot oats
the setter's reading: British slang for a jail sentence, as in 'doing' it

explanation.walkthrough: Porridge is an oat breakfast, and in British slang 'doing porridge' means serving time in prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Porridge is both a breakfast dish and slang for a prison sentence.

clue.text: Aussie native runs round and round

blocks.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
each round is the round letter O

explanation.surface: An Australian animal keeps running in circles.
explanation.walkthrough: The circling is two O shapes, not a movement.
explanation.definitionFit: Roo is Australian short for kangaroo, a native animal.

clue.text: Almost losing head at dawn?

indicators.note: the word loses its head, its first letter

blocks.note: NEARLY (almost) without its first letter N

explanation.surface: Someone nearly loses their head at first light, like a dawn execution.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that dawn is only one example of early.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done at dawn is done early in the day.

clue.text: Last of weather holding me up

blocks.note: rain is a kind of weather
as printed, then reversed to EM

explanation.surface: The final bit of bad weather is delaying me.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last of weather' looks like a last-letter instruction, but Last is the definition and of only links it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to last is to go on existing, to stay, as in 'the snow will last all week'.

clue.text: Careless about failure

blocks.note: re means about, concerning
a miss is a failure to hit

explanation.surface: Someone is not bothered about having failed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as part of the phrase careless about; it is RE.
explanation.definitionFit: Remiss means careless in one's duty.

clue.text: Former Lothario hoards red wine

indicators.note: the phrase hoards the answer, keeping it inside

blocks.note: forMER LOThario

explanation.surface: An ageing seducer has been stockpiling red wine.
explanation.walkthrough: A Lothario is a womaniser; the name is here only for its first three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the grape, originally from Bordeaux, gives its name to one of the most widely drunk red wines.

clue.text: Couple I encountered on way back

indicators.note: met on the way back runs in the opposite direction

blocks.note: as printed
met = encountered

explanation.surface: Someone bumps into a pair of people while heading home.
explanation.walkthrough: The meeting on the way home is the wordplay: I, then MET travelling backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal sense: two people seen together romantically are said to be 'an item', a single unit of gossip.

clue.text: Tory I rip off is most pressing concern

indicators.note: letters that are off are not right, so their order must change

blocks.note: the eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A politician's top worry is that someone will copy a Conservative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rip off' reads as plagiarise; off is the signal to rearrange TORY I RIP. A Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: A priority is the thing that most urgently needs attention.

clue.text: Periodically protect man of letters

indicators.note: periodically means at regular intervals, so every other letter

blocks.note: the odd letters of PrOtEcT

explanation.surface: From time to time a writer needs to be shielded.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'man of letters' is also, literally, a man made from letters picked out of protect.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: 'man of letters' is an old phrase for a literary writer, and a verse writer is one kind.

clue.text: Outsiders expelled from Athens at that time

indicators.note: the outer letters are thrown out of the word

blocks.note: ATHENS without its outer letters A and S

explanation.surface: Foreigners were banished from ancient Athens back in those days.
explanation.walkthrough: The ostracism of ancient Athens is the picture; the outsiders are just the first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the adverb, pointing back to a moment already mentioned, as in 'we lived in Athens then'.

clue.text: Resident gullible about start of trouble

blocks.note: naive = gullible
first letter of trouble

explanation.surface: A trusting local is uneasy about the first sign of trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as concerning; here it wraps NAIVE around T.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: someone born in a place and living there, where a resident need only live there.

clue.text: Shopkeeper selling food increasingly vulgar, I hear

indicators.note: what I hear is the sound of the word, not its spelling

blocks.note: the comparative of gross, coarse; the sound is kept and respelt

explanation.surface: Rumour says the food shop owner is getting ever cruder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Increasingly' asks for a comparative: GROSSER, more gross.
explanation.definitionFit: A grocer is a shopkeeper who sells food and household goods.
